text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementHistoryOldest Evidence of Human Cannabis Use Has a Ghoulish TwistTake a ride with the spectral cavalcadeJCBy Jake Currie1:00 PM CST on November 5, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleA group of horses is called a “herd,” unless they’ve been ritually sacrificed. Then they’re called a “spectral cavalcade.” The term comes from writings of the Greek historian Herodotus describing the funerary practice of the Scythians, a group of nomadic horseback riders that roamed the Central Asian steppes until around the third century BCE. Powered By 10 ShareNextStayOf course, not all of Herodotus’ records were accurate (he mentioned dog-sized ants that harvested gold, for example), but the spectral cavalcade turned out to be (literally) dead on. Archaeologists discovered burial mounds in southern Siberia topped with the cadavers of sacrificed horses. Now, beneath the spectral cavalcade, they’ve discovered something else Herodotus was right about: The Scythians used cannabis as part of their funeral rites.Read more: “What Goes on in the Brain When a Good Buzz Gets Harshed”Already have an account?Log inRead without limitsFinish this story and enjoy unlimited, ad-free access to Nautilus.
